en: The Sūtra on Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma for King Udayana,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
The flavor of sensual pleasure is extremely slight, while the afflictions of sorrow and suffering are exceedingly many.
Therefore, the wise person should cultivate skillful means to swiftly distance themselves from all desires and diligently practice pure conduct.
I have heard that in the past, there was a prince named Udayana, son of a thousand blessings, who succeeded his father to the throne and resided in the city of Kauśāmbī.

That city was exceptionally wonderful, vast, and pure; its palaces and towers shone with brilliant splendor and were exquisitely adorned, while its windows and lattices were open and airy, draped with networks of pearls.
This city is adorned with thousands of millions of towers and pavilions.
Its streets and lanes intersect at right angles, its thoroughfares are orderly and uniform, and its marketplaces are filled with abundance and many rare treasures.

Surrounding the city are excellent groves and gardens where trees are lush and verdant, flowers and fruits flourish, and streams flow with purity, producing many lotuses whose blue, yellow, red, and white hues reflect one another.
Swans, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, parrots, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas warbled in harmony like the sounds of music.
Its magnificent splendor was like that of the king of mountains, Kailāsa, adorned with lofty crags and precipitous peaks, and it resembled the city of Sudarśana, the abode of Śakra.

King Udayana was handsome in appearance and endowed with majestic marks; he was intelligent and wise, possessed peerless martial valor, and was fully equipped with all arts and skills, such that there was nothing he did not know.
He was skilled at enchanting elephants, causing all the mountain elephants to assemble at his command; furthermore, he could control them so that they were all tamed and obedient.
He was also skilled at playing the lute, with music harmonious, elegant, and rhythmic, where the *gong* and *shang* notes were perfectly attuned, such that birds and beasts danced in unison.
He compounded fragrant pills to subdue enemies; wherever the fragrance reached, all came to submit and obey.
He was highly skilled at carving and painting, capturing the likeness with perfect accuracy; the images he produced were no different from the actual forms themselves.

He was fully proficient in all sixty-two arts; yet regarding clothing and food, he did not prize abundance or luxury. He commended the poor and honored the elderly, showing compassion and relief to the common people. He governed the state with the True Dharma, never wearying day or night. His rites, ceremonies, laws, and regulations followed the ancient classics exactly, like those of the former sage-kings such as Śaśāda and others. The country was wealthy and the population prosperous, with treasuries overflowing. Persons of merit and virtue gathered to be born in that land; receiving the King’s transformative influence, they all cultivated goodness.

They were extensively learned in the scriptures and commentaries, clearly understanding all treatises, and there were none among the worldly classics in which they were not thoroughly practiced. They were brave, robust, and martial, like Rāma and Añjana.
Due to the roots of goodness planted by the King in a previous life as a Pratyekabuddha, he has obtained such a reward.
The King’s majestic virtue causes neighboring states to stand in awe and submission; his transformative influence shines forth, its fame heard throughout the world.
At that time, there was a son of the prime minister named Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja.

His appearance was exceptionally handsome and rare in the world; he was intelligent, wise, widely learned, and possessed great erudition. He was benevolent and universally loving, with a resolve to relieve suffering. He exhorted and transformed the people of the kingdom so that they all practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, took faith and delight in the Triple Gem, left the household life to study the Way, and attained the fruit of full ordination.
Wandering about to teach and transform others, he returned to the city of Kauśāmbī, intending to deliver his kinsmen; he went everywhere to beg for alms.
Having finished his begging, he sat cross-legged beneath a tree in the forest and entered meditative concentration through contemplation.
At that time, there was a man who recognized Piṇḍola; he came and addressed the king, saying:
"The former son of the prime minister, Piṇḍola, is currently nearby here, beneath a tree in this forest."

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and felt deep reverence; he immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and set out for the Venerable One’s dwelling, accompanied by his palace ladies, retinue, and servants.
After the greetings were concluded, he invited the king to take his seat.
The king then reflected:
"Whatever matters I have in doubt, I shall now inquire about them.
And he spoke these words:
“Piṇḍola! Now I have known you since we were young; your ancestors served as prime ministers in former lives, being wise, intelligent, and far-reaching, and always acting as national preceptors.”
"Now that we have met, I wish to ask about matters of doubt; it is not intended to cause you any offense.
Will you explain them to me?
The Venerable One replied:
“Ask whatever you wish, and I shall analyze and explain it for the sake of the King.
The King asked in verse:
“All people in the world, / Greedily attached to the five desires, / Indulge their passions and are heedless.”
To find delight therein—
for you now, dwelling alone in seclusion and having abandoned affection and love, what honor or pleasure is there?
The Venerable replied:
"I observe that all causes and conditions are entirely impermanent; for this reason, I have gone forth.
Having severed emotional attachments, I delight in the forest thickets like a wild deer."

Devoting myself with diligence to practice, I have forever severed the afflictions; with the axe of wisdom, I have shattered the branches of the tree of craving. My mind is free from attachment, the poisonous fruits are extinguished, and I have crossed over the torrential river of birth and death with its swift currents of all fetters; henceforth, there is no more sorrow or distress.
"It is like a flying bird that escapes from a net and soars far away through the void; this is called liberation.
Upon hearing these words, the king said to Piṇḍola:

"Now my power is able to subdue all nations, and my majestic virtue shines brilliantly like the midday sun. Adorned with a celestial crown, wearing magnificent necklaces and fine garments, and attended by court ladies, I am like Śakra, the Lord of Devas."
"As you now dwell alone, do you perhaps envy me?
The Venerable replied,
"I have no heart of envy."
The king asked again:
"For what reason do you not wish for or envy me?
The Venerable One replied:

"Today, the mud of my worldly existence has dried up; all fetters of becoming have now been liberated. I feel no envy even for the exquisite celestial maidens of Śakra, let alone for you, who are but base and defiled mortals!"

What wise person, having attained liberation from the bonds of Māra, crossed the shore of birth and death, obtained the pure eye of wisdom, and destroyed the darkness of ignorance, would envy the king?
How could one with clear vision envy a blind man?
What person who is strong and healthy would envy the sick?
What person who is without guilt would envy a prisoner?
What person who is immensely wealthy would envy the poor?
What noble person would envy a slave?
What wise person would envy one who is foolish?
What brave and strong person would envy one who is weak and feeble?
Having heard this, the king was filled with distress and spoke these words:
"How can your metaphor be so bitter and extreme!
Could I truly be so wretched and inferior as that?"
The Venerable One replied:

"Your Majesty lacks the eye of wisdom; you are afflicted by the defilements and swept away by the swift current of the four graspings. You have lost your courage and vigor, and are unable to apply yourself with diligence."
One who is thus infantile and ignorant, failing to recognize the ultimate truth and sinking into the ocean of suffering, is the lot of such a king.
To conceive thoughts of rarity regarding the five desires is truly contrary to pure conduct.
The King asked again,
"What fault is there such that you say it is a transgression?
The Venerable One replied:

"These five desires are the root of all suffering; they destroy the roots of goodness possessed by sentient beings like hail destroying seedlings. They sting and afflict sentient beings more severely than venomous snakes; they burn away merit like a blazing fire; they deceive and delude ordinary people like a mirage; and they bewilder and confuse those who are deluded like a magical illusion."

Desire seeks to feign intimacy more treacherously than an enemy; it is like an old ox sinking into the mire; it is like a great net ensnaring the three realms; it is like a path of swords difficult to tread upon; it is capable of binding, confining, and slaughtering sentient beings—all calamities and afflictions arise from desire.
In ancient times, there was a Vasu deity who, due to the causes and conditions of desire, was bound by the asura Bali and cast into boiling water.

The Deva Bala destroyed the city walls of the Asuras, exterminating their people and afflicting the royal lineage of King Kharaskandha; he utterly annihilated the eight Cūḍapanthaka kings and their hundred sons.
The Asura Bhīṣma harmed the thousand-eyed Rāma, as well as the ten-headed Rākṣasa and a multitude of several hundred billion Rākṣasas.

Rāvaṇa harmed Indra and the king of Yakṣas; King Mārīci exterminated the clan of Drumakinnara; King Kārtavīrya was killed by the Brahmin Jamadagni; Vināśana harmed the kinsmen of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and the five sons of Bāṇa killed eighteen hundred million people, including the royal lineages of Pāṇḍu, Anudatta, Caṅga, Kuru, and Mithilā-Dhāntaka.
"These kings of men, all for the sake of desire, destroy one another.
He then spoke in verse:
"Though the royal throne is honorable and majestic, Its succession does not pause for even a moment."
As fleeting as a flash of lightning, it returns to extinction in an instant.
Though the sovereignty of a king brings ultimate wealth and ease, the fool’s mind delights in it;
yet when the time of decay and death arrives, his suffering is more intense than that of the lowly.
The king occupies a high station, his fame fills the four quarters;
he is upright and most lovely, adorning his body in various ways—
yet he is like one facing death, wearing flower garlands and jeweled necklaces.
With little life remaining, the royal throne is likewise so.
A king is like a crow, always harboring various fears;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—at all times—[he remains thus].
Amidst those both near and distant, he is always possessed of a mind of doubt and fear.
His ministers, subjects, palace ladies, and consorts, as well as elephants, horses, and precious treasures—
all that exists within the realm is the property of the king.
When all kings lay down their lives, they abandon everything and nothing follows them.
Whether it be kings of men, kings of gods, or kings of asuras,
though they wield power over the people and slaughter one another with axes and halberds, [nothing remains].
Failing to recognize impermanence and suffering, they recklessly increase their greed, envy, and affliction.
It is like a grove of exquisite flowers where a golden serpent sleeps;
the foolish take it for a precious treasure, wrap it up, and carry it home.
The serpent’s awakening unleashes a fire of venom that incinerates its own dwelling.
Sovereignty is like a grove of flowers; calamity is like a golden serpent.
The foolish deem it noble, but the wise find no pleasure in it.
Just as when a lump of meat is placed at a crossroads, foxes, wolves,
crows, vultures, and the like vie with one another to scramble for it and eat it,
so too is the position of a king: the multitude contends together to seize it.
Birds and beasts use their beaks and claws to claw, tear, and contend together;
kings use swords and spears to harm one another and dispute for positions of honor.
They are just like those birds and beasts; there is no difference between them and the ignorant.
I would rather eat ash and earth, or subsist on grass and vegetables.
This body is like a festering sore; it will inevitably reach a state of putrefaction.
Why, for the sake of this, should I commit various evil deeds?
Like eating the *kimpāka* fruit, its fragrance and flavor are fully present;
yet when that fruit is digested, the body is utterly ruined.
Sovereignty is like that fruit: once lost, it gives rise to suffering and distress.
Suppose there is a land where pestilence and disease prevail;
wise and superior persons should swiftly distance themselves from it.
If they do not distance themselves, it is like holding a torch against the wind.
If one does not relinquish them, one will surely burn oneself;
it is like a thirsty person drinking salt water—there is never a time of satisfaction.
Because of the causes and conditions of desire, one [neglects] the city, the citadel, and one's kinsmen.
They were utterly destroyed, leaving nothing behind.
Though there were a hundred brothers, because of the causes and conditions of desire,
they too were all completely ruined and extinguished.
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra—such kings as these were all destroyed by desire.

"One should know that a kingdom is like a net, like a snare, like deep mud, like a whirlpool, and like the waves of the ocean; it is like a forest on fire, like a precarious cliff, and like hell. What wise person would delight in craving and attachment?"
Such is this great suffering; what wise person would conceive the notion of pleasure therein? O Great King!
Alas, how strange it is! To be thus deceived!
To be deceived to such an extent!
It is like an empty fist deceiving a small child; it is as swift and unceasing as a magical illusion. The deception of the five desires is likewise so.

It is like a monkey on the peak of a high mountain who, seeing clouds spread across the sky, mistakes them for solid ground; thinking it to be earth, he throws himself down, falling from a cliff a hundred fathoms high and losing his life, with his entire body shattered to pieces.
It is also like a jackal who, seeing a *citraka* tree whose fruit resembles meat, goes to eat it as soon as it sees it fall to the ground; realizing it is not meat, he further thinks:
"This is not meat."
"Whatever is on that tree must surely be meat.
He then stayed there to guard it and was consequently distressed by it.
The way the five desires deceive the king is just like this.
It is also like a merchant who deceives people with counterfeit pearls; the way the five desires deceive a king is likewise.

Furthermore, it is like an infant or a fool who craves flavors and greedily longs for a joy-pill (*modaka*); when someone approaches him with a lump of clay to deceive him, he takes it to be real and runs after it in weary exhaustion until he finally obtains the lump of clay—just as a mirage deceives a thirsty fool during the heat of the day.
It is just as when a group of people erects a magic pillar before them, enabling the assembly at that time to see various phenomena;
yet if the magic pillar is pulled out, the forms and images immediately vanish, like a master painter or a mechanic.

It is like a dog barking at its own reflection in a well; with eyes wide with rage and hair bristling, it thinks the shadow at the bottom of the well wishes to fight with it, and out of this groundless fury, it leaps into the well and dies.
"Great King!
You should observe this well: how could there be anything among the five desires that is permanent?
How could there be any royal throne that remains for long?"
Since even the majestic power and influence of the honored and noble cannot remain,
what realm could exist without undergoing change and decay?
What precious treasure could exist without being lost and scattered?
What sensual pleasure can there be that is permanent and unchanging?
Whatever is bestowed by suffering must inevitably undergo decay and destruction.
What union can there be that does not end in separation?
The essential nature of all five desires is truly suffering; it is only through deluded imagination that they give rise to pleasure.
What conditioned phenomena are there that do not resemble a plantain tree or a city of the Gandharvas?
"Great King!

While dwelling amidst the oppression of birth, old age, sickness, death, decline, calamity, and terror, how can you conceive a sense of attachment and delight toward the meager pleasures of your kingdom?"

It is like a deer in a forest with fire breaking out on all four sides; like a bird in a cage; like a fish in a net; like a tortoise that has swallowed a hook; like a lion whose heart has been pierced by a poisoned arrow; like a dragon dwelling in a field of incantations; like a person inside a house with fire breaking out on all four sides; like being in a dilapidated and decaying flower-palace that is about to collapse suddenly; or like a beautiful lotus pond where a water-rākṣasa seizes and devours people.
He spoke again in verse:
"The afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death—within these you are not yet liberated;
the poisoned arrows of ignorance and craving have still not been extracted."
O Emperor of Men, how can you give rise to thoughts of pleasure and attachment?
Like an elephant dwelling in a forest while great fires break out on all four sides,
how can there be any joy while situated in such a place of urgent peril?
Great King, you should know that glory and rank are but momentary;
the wise observe this deeply and should not conceive of such things as being rare or marvelous.
Why do you misunderstand?
You are truly a slave to craving, yet you conceive the notion of being noble;
you have abandoned supreme and wondrous treasures, yet you conceive the notion of being immensely wealthy.
Lacking skillful means, one falsely conceives the notion of wisdom;
Afflicted by the maladies of various defilements, one falsely conceives the notion of being free from illness;
Not yet having emerged from the womb of birth and death, one falsely conceives the notion of fearlessness.
"Abiding amidst the thicket of the twelve sense-bases, one falsely conceives of them as being without thorns;
when the thieves of desire plunder the faculties, one falsely conceives of them as being without thieves.
Great King!"
Yet this body must inevitably return to decay; high status, nobility, and glory must inevitably decline and perish; and wealth, treasures, and storehouses must inevitably be lost and dispersed.
Great King!
As the Buddha has said:
"Glory and rank are like a dream; the bonds of affection are but temporary.
Yet you conceive of the five desires as something rare and difficult to encounter; how, then, can one of virtuous character be said to have practiced skillful observation regarding this?
Why is this? Prosperity, rank, and the bonds of affection must inevitably end in separation, just as a flock of birds roost together on a single tree at night but scatter in four directions at dawn;
or like a guest house, where guests gather in the evening but each departs by a different road at daybreak.
It is also like people traveling by boat together; once they have reached the shore, each takes their own separate path.
It is also like many pieces of wood gathered together by a swift current, which in an instant are dispersed by the flow.
They are like drifting clouds, dispersing and vanishing in an instant.
Where music is performed, men and women gather; once the music has ended, they each disperse.
Though palace ladies and court maidsens are upright and exquisite, the principle of impermanence applies: having met, they must eventually be abandoned.
It is like a flowering tree upon which bees gather; when the flowers wither and fall away, the bees depart.
It is like a lotus pond that has dried up, which female elephants will no longer enter.
It is like a great lake where cranes delight to dwell and roam, yet once it has run dry, they no longer approach it.
In a household where merit is exhausted, honor and profit do not draw near.
It is like dense clouds gathering where flashes of lightning appear for but a moment;
yet when the wind blows away the clouds, the lightning does not appear.
He will not abandon you, yet you must certainly abandon him.
It is like when summer ends, the peacock's plumage sheds itself entirely;
it is like when the cold season arrives, the wild geese and cranes depart for distant lakes.
It is like the *aśoka* tree: when its flowers and leaves are in full bloom, people cherish and delight in it;
yet when they wither and decay, and the flowers and leaves are gone, no one looks upon it.
It is also like a floral banner: those of noble status love and revere it, but once the flowers have wilted and the threads are severed, they cast it aside.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Impermanent and not solid, Like a plantain tree or a bubble of water, And like scattered clouds;
Such is the exalted and sovereign rank of the Heavenly King."
Perilous and fragile, it is likewise so.
O Emperor of Men, you should know that the pursuit of gain is exceedingly swift, like water rushing down into a deep valley;
sensual desire is extremely light and rapid, shifting and turning like a dangling rope.
"Deluded and defiled by desire, they fail to realize that this leads to their downfall.
The Venerable One said,
"Great King!"
I shall now briefly provide an analogy for the King regarding the faults and perils of attachment to the flavors of birth and death;

may Your Majesty listen with a sincere mind. Long ago, there was a man traveling on a desolate road who encountered a great, vicious elephant. Pursued by the elephant, he fled in frantic terror, finding no place of refuge. Seeing a dilapidated well, he immediately climbed a tree and entered the well to hide himself. A white and a black rat were gnawing at the tree root, and on the four sides of this well were four venomous snakes wishing to bite him; furthermore, beneath the well dwelt a great poisonous dragon.

On his left he fears four snakes, and below he fears a venomous dragon; the tree upon which he leans has its roots shaking. Three drops of honey fall from the tree into his mouth. At that moment, the tree shakes and crushes a bee hive; the swarms of bees fly out in all directions, stinging and biting the man. A wild fire breaks out and comes to burn the tree as well.
"Great King, you should know that the suffering and distress of that person are beyond measure.
The King, filled with sorrow and aversion, said:
"That person obtains very little flavor, yet endures immense suffering and affliction."

That which they savor is like water in a cow’s footprint, while their suffering and affliction are like the great ocean; the flavor is like a mustard seed, while the suffering is like Mount Sumeru; the flavor is like a firefly, while the suffering is like the sun and moon; it is as if comparing the hollows of a lotus root to the vast void, or as if comparing a mosquito to a garuḍa—such is the disparity between the extent of their flavor and their bitter affliction.
The Venerable One said:
"Great King!
The wilderness is a metaphor for birth and death."
That man represents the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
the elephant represents impermanence (*anityatā*);
and the pit by the mound represents the human body.
The tree root is a metaphor for human life.
The white and black rats are metaphors for day and night.
Their gnawing at the tree root is a metaphor for the moment-to-moment cessation [of existence].
The four venomous snakes are a metaphor for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The honey is a metaphor for the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
The swarm of bees is a metaphor for evil discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Being burned by a wild fire is a metaphor for old age;
subduing the venomous dragon is a metaphor for death.
Therefore, one should know that the flavor of desire is extremely slight, while its suffering and afflictions are exceedingly many.

Birth, old age, sickness, and death exercise their power over all people; the people of the world suffer physical and mental toil with no place of refuge. Harassed by manifold sufferings as fleeting as lightning, this is a cause for sorrow and should not be clung to with attachment.
"Great King!
What I am now saying to you, though the words may be harsh and unpleasant, is truly for your benefit.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s hair stood on end; grief and joy welled up within him, and he wept with flowing tears.
He immediately rose, joined his palms, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"I am childish and ignorant, lacking in wisdom; being of lowly station, I have uttered such deluded words. Please accept my repentance for these deluded words."
The Venerable One said:
"I have now gone forth through patience; there is nothing I do not endure.
My mind is pure, like the autumn moon free from the veil of clouds."
"The King now repents; may it be granted that Your Majesty, like Śakra, the Lord of Devas, shall attain the traces of the Path.
The King was greatly delighted and, together with his retinue, paid homage and returned to the palace.
The Sūtra on Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma for King Udayana.
